newsitem.title: USA: Florida governor pledges help for Haiti.
newsitem.headline: Florida governor pledges help for Haiti.

text.p: Florida's governor unveiled a state-sponsored plan on Thursday to help bolster Haiti's economy and improve government institutions within the fledgling Caribbean democracy.

The Florida/Haiti Initiative, a public and private effort to improve health care, education and business opportunities within Haiti, marks a new level of cooperation between the state and the poorest nation in the western hemisphere.

"A stable Caribbean is good for a stable Florida," said Gov. Lawton Chiles, flanked at a news conference by a delegation from Haiti's legislature. "It is in our best interest to promote a strong economy and democracy in Haiti."

Haiti's first democratically elected president, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, was overthrown in a bloody military coup just eight months after his 1991 inauguration and was restored to power three years later after a multinational military intervention.
Florida, the closest U.S. state to Haiti, has been hit in recent years by Haiti's political and economic unrest as thousands of refugees streamed to U.S. shores.

"Of all the states, Florida has the most important ties to Haiti, not just refugees and immigration but also significant business interests," said Terry McCoy of the University of Florida's Centre for Latin American Studies. "It's not just Florida giving to Haiti. Florida is benefitting too."
Organisers said the Florida/Haiti Initiative, using more than $250,000 in federal and state funds, is a largely volunteer effort to match U.S. groups and individuals to Haitian organisations.
"A strong democracy in Haiti is the best way we can protect Florida against any other massive immigration exodus," Chiles said. "We certainly want to do that."
During their three-day visit, Haitian delegates will meet with business leaders, educators, health care providers and government officials to study how U.S.institutions operate.
Garry Guiteau, first secretary of the Haitian Chamber of Deputies, said such exchanges are critical to the Caribbean nation, which is the region's newest democracy.
"The world in which we live today is very interconnected," Guiteau said through an interpreter. "Everyone has to help his neighbour. And today, more than ever, Haiti needs your help."
